blocks.text: Industrial-era knowledge changed through more than additional discoveries. Organizations could continually train researchers. Societies, journals, universities, laboratories and engineering institutions allowed methods and records to accumulate beyond individual lives.

Mass education widened access to shared knowledge and discipline, while capital supported long-term investment in machines, railways and factories. Knowledge, work and finance were connected; industrial development cannot be explained solely through a genius or a fortune.

These capabilities did not enter identical institutional relationships everywhere. Arrangements among states, banks, firms, land and labor shaped how resources were organized, returns distributed and costs borne.

The spread of science, education and capital therefore did not erase industrial differences. Similar tools entered different historical structures and formed different combinations. Crossing related energy and production thresholds did not provide every society with one institutional answer.
